fact: Carpenter Avenue is named for Stephen V. R. Carpenter, a landowner in the Wakefield section of the Bronx who bought property there from Mary Duryea in 1868. His family name was later applied to the street as the farmland was subdivided into a streetcar suburb.
namesake: Stephen V. R. Carpenter, Wakefield landowner

fact: Willis Avenue is named for Edward Willis, a Bronx real estate businessman of the 1860s who lived nearby on Alexander Avenue. The street opened in his honor in 1897, replacing what had been the main road through the old village of Morrisania.
source_label: Historical Marker Database, Willis Avenue Bridge

fact: Clintonville Street is named for DeWitt Clinton, the New York governor, mayor and senator who lived in the area when Whitestone was briefly renamed Clintonville in his honor during the 19th century. The neighborhood reverted to the name Whitestone, but the street kept the Clintonville name.
namesake: DeWitt Clinton, New York governor and mayor

fact: Davidson Avenue is named for Colonel Mathias Oliver Davidson, who served as the Bronx Chief Engineer of Streets from 1867 to 1872 and owned land in the Fordham area. Before settling in the Bronx, Davidson had prospected for gold in Arizona and worked as a civil engineer in Cuba and the American Southwest.
namesake: Colonel Mathias Oliver Davidson, Chief Engineer of Streets

fact: Edgemere Avenue takes its name from the Edgemere Hotel, built in 1895 by developer Frederick J. Lancaster, who chose the name as old English for edge of the sea. Lancaster had first tried calling the area New Venice, but that name never caught on with residents.
namesake: the Edgemere Hotel, old English for edge of the sea

fact: Alexander Avenue is reputed to be named for Alexander Bathgate, a Scottish immigrant who worked as overseer of the Morris family farm in the early 19th century before saving enough money to buy part of the land himself. Bathgate also gave his name to the nearby Bathgate section of the Bronx.
namesake: Alexander Bathgate, overseer of the Morris manor
source_label: Brick Underground, Alexander Avenue Bronx history

fact: Bay Ridge Parkway takes its name from the Bay Ridge neighborhood it runs through. The area was called Yellow Hook until 1853, when residents renamed it Bay Ridge for the glacial ridge overlooking New York Bay, after yellow fever outbreaks made the old name unpopular.
source_label: Brownstoner, Bay Ridge Brooklyn name origin

fact: Alameda Avenue is named for the Spanish word alameda, meaning a promenade lined with poplar trees. The term came into general use in Spain in the 16th century for tree lined malls and was later applied to this Queens street even though other tree species eventually replaced the original poplars.
namesake: the Spanish word alameda, a poplar lined promenade

fact: Tiffany Street is named for H. D. Tiffany, a 19th century landowner in the Hunts Point section of the Bronx whose name appears on streets and monuments throughout the area. The intersecting Fox Street honors his father in law, William H. Fox.

North Burgher Avenue is named for the Burgher family, prominent landowners on Staten Island's southeast shore. David Burgher, a Stapleton fisherman who was appointed Deputy Sheriff in 1833, was elected a trustee of the Village of Edgewater in 1867.
namesake: the Burgher family of Staten Island
source_label: NYC Landmarks Preservation Commission, Mary and David Burgher House designation report

fact: Rutland Road is named for Rutland, a small county in the East Midlands of England. Brooklyn renamed the street, originally called Tulip Street, in 1897 as part of a broader trend of giving local streets genteel British place names.
source_label: Forgotten New York, Rutland Road, Lefferts Gardens

fact: Mill Road in the Bath Beach section of Brooklyn is named for two grist mills that once stood along its route, making it a main artery of the area for roughly two centuries. By 1889 the unpaved lane also held a hotel and a yacht club before losing its importance to the modern street grid.
namesake: two grist mills that once stood along the road
source_label: Forgotten New York, Mill Road, twilit lane of Bath Beach

fact: Brighton Beach Avenue is named for Brighton, the English seaside resort, an allusion chosen by developer William Engeman when he built the Hotel Brighton on the site in the 1870s. He hoped the name would draw wealthy New York vacationers seeking a prestigious beach destination.
source_label: Brownstoner, Brighton Beach Brooklyn neighborhood name history

fact: Vleigh Place takes its name from the Dutch word vly, meaning a marshy meadow. The Kew Gardens Hills area was known to Dutch settlers as the Head of Vleigh, and the street is the only one in New York City whose name begins with the letters VL.
namesake: the Dutch word vly, a marshy meadow

fact: Cooper Square is named for Peter Cooper, the industrialist, inventor and philanthropist who founded Cooper Union nearby to offer free education. The square was renamed in his honor after his death in 1883, and a monument by Augustus Saint-Gaudens now stands at its center.

Wilson Street is named for James Wilson, a signer of the Declaration of Independence. The street was mapped around 1846 as part of a cluster of Williamsburg streets that Brooklyn named to honor the signers.
namesake: James Wilson, signer of the Declaration of Independence

fact: Harding Avenue is named for President Warren G. Harding, honored when developers platted the surrounding bungalow colony in the Throggs Neck section of the Bronx during his presidency in the 1920s. The tract was marketed as a summer retreat along the water for working class New Yorkers.
